pro_tips: Camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine (~7,800 ft) to stage a lighter, faster summit push
Favor the Access Creek approach over the Luna Creek bushwhack
Budget roughly 6-7 hours up and 5-6 hours down from high camp
Carry 3-4 flukes/pickets — parties have placed four on the glacier section alone
before.approach: There are two real approach options for the South (Southwest) Route on Phantom Peak, and both are serious multi-day North Cascades bushwhacks — this is not a trail hike. Option one, the Luna Creek approach: from Ross Lake Resort, take the water taxi across Ross Lake (roughly $35, saves about 6 miles of paddling/road-walking) to the Big Beaver trailhead. From there it's about 14 miles of maintained, mostly flat, forested trail up the Big Beaver Creek drainage (through old-growth cedar groves and past beaver ponds/marshy sections) to Luna Camp, an established backcountry campsite where a NOCA wilderness permit is required. From Luna Camp the trail effectively ends; climbers leave the maintained tread and push cross-country up the Luna Creek drainage toward Phantom Peak's south side, gaining roughly 4,000+ ft over a few miles through some of the worst brush in the Cascades. Fred Beckey, on the first traverse through here in 1940, called it 'the worst imaginable struggle with flies, devil's club, willows, and alder' — modern parties confirm little has changed, reporting huckleberry, devil's club, vine maple and slide alder so dense that 0.5 mph is a good pace, plus heavy mosquito/fly pressure in summer. The creek itself must be forded in places; fords get harder (deeper, faster) the lower/farther downstream you are, so it's best to gain elevation out of the valley bottom as early as possible rather than fighting the brush along the creek itself. Water is abundant throughout (the creek and countless side-seeps), but hazard is really the terrain: no trail, no cairns, high fall-into-a-hole-in-the-brush risk, and real potential to get separated from a partner in the thick stuff (this has happened to real parties here). Above the brush line the drainage opens into subalpine meadow and talus below Phantom's south aspect. Option two, favored by several recent parties, comes from the north via Whatcom Pass: Hannegan Trailhead (3,100 ft) → Ruth Creek Trail → Chilliwack River Trail (includes a cable-car creek crossing) → Brush Creek Trail up to Whatcom Pass, then off-trail via the Whatcom Glacier and Perfect Pass to a base camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine. From that camp, the route to Phantom itself is a roughly 1,000-ft descending traverse east across snow/talus to the base of Phantom's broad southwest buttress, then up a snowfield to a saddle around 6,100 ft within the buttress — this saddle is effectively the start of the technical climbing. Whichever approach is used, expect 2-3 days of travel each way; the total round-trip distance (51.5 km / ~32 mi) reflects the Big Beaver/Luna Creek option's mileage.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, Whatcom Pass and Perfect Pass to a camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine
approach_variants.notes: The northern option, favoured by several recent parties. From the Hannegan Trailhead at 3,100 ft, the Hannegan Pass Trail leads over the pass to the Chilliwack River Trail, which includes a cable-car crossing, then up the Brush Creek Trail to Whatcom Pass. From there the route leaves trail and goes off-trail via the Whatcom Glacier and Perfect Pass to a base camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine. Expect 2-3 days of travel each way.
hazards: A bergschrund on the summit snow finger, crossed via a slabby rock step
Somewhat rotten rock on the summit tower and gully section, with natural anchors only
Rockfall off the buttress walls onto the snow finger
A 1,000 ft descending traverse that has to be regained on the return
The Chilliwack cable-car crossing and the Whatcom Glacier traverse on the way in
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START OF THE CLIMBING IS A SADDLE INSIDE THE BUTTRESS, AT ABOUT 6,100 FT, AND YOU GET THERE BY LOSING HEIGHT FIRST. From the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp, the way to Phantom is a roughly 1,000 FT DESCENDING TRAVERSE EAST across snow and talus to the base of Phantom's broad southwest buttress, then up a snowfield to a saddle around 6,100 ft WITHIN the buttress. That saddle is effectively the start of the technical climbing.

SO THE TEST IN CLOUD IS THE SHAPE OF THE GROUND, NOT THE VIEW: you go DOWN and EAST for a thousand feet, then UP a snowfield, and you stop when the snowfield delivers you into a gap in a rock rib rather than onto open mountainside. A saddle inside a buttress has rock rising on both sides of you; open snow does not.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing the descending traverse east past the buttress toe drops you toward Luna Cirque and the ground the peak's other route uses, which is a different climb from a different camp.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB: above the saddle the route takes a pocket glacier and snowfield to a bergschrund crossed by a slabby rock step, then a snow finger, then broken class 2-3 rock to a false summit and a short exposed step to the true summit. One bergschrund, one snow finger, one false summit. If you have crossed two schrunds you are not on this line.

approach_variants.name: Big Beaver Trail to Luna Camp, then the Luna Creek bushwhack up Phantom's south side
approach_variants.notes: The line the recorded distance reflects. From Ross Lake Resort, take the water taxi across Ross Lake, roughly $35 and saving about 6 miles, to the Big Beaver trailhead. From there it is about 14 miles of maintained, mostly flat, forested trail up the Big Beaver Creek drainage through old-growth cedar and past beaver ponds to Luna Camp, an established backcountry site where a wilderness permit is required. From Luna Camp the trail effectively ends. Climbers leave the tread and push cross-country up the Luna Creek drainage toward Phantom's south side, gaining roughly 4,000 ft over a few miles through some of the worst brush in the Cascades. Modern parties report huckleberry, devil's club, vine maple and slide alder dense enough that half a mile an hour is a good pace, with heavy insect pressure.
hazards: Some of the worst brush in the Cascades, at roughly half a mile an hour, with devil's club and slide alder
Fords of Luna Creek that get harder the lower you are
High risk of falling into a hole hidden by brush, and of separating from a partner
Heavy mosquito and fly pressure in summer
No trail, no cairns and real disorientation on the way back down
approach_variants.baseFinding:
IN THIS DRAINAGE THE NAVIGATION RULE IS ABOUT HEIGHT, NOT DIRECTION, AND IT IS THE ONE THING THAT MAKES THE DAY WORK. The creek must be forded in places, and FORDS GET HARDER THE LOWER AND FARTHER DOWNSTREAM YOU ARE. Gain elevation out of the valley bottom as early as you can rather than fighting the brush along the creek. If you are still beside running water after a couple of hours, you are on the losing line.

ARRIVAL, WHICH IS UNAMBIGUOUS EVEN WITH NO VISIBILITY: above the brush line the drainage OPENS into subalpine meadow and talus below Phantom's south aspect. The brush stopping is the signal. Nothing else in this valley changes character that completely.

FROM THERE THE BASE TEST IS THE SAME ONE THE NORTHERN APPROACH USES: find the snowfield that leads up into a saddle at about 6,100 ft within the southwest buttress. That gap is where the technical climbing starts.

A REAL RISK PECULIAR TO THIS APPROACH, RECORDED BECAUSE IT HAS HAPPENED: in brush this thick, parties have become separated from each other. Agree a regrouping rule before entering it, not during.

weather.typical: Short summer weather window, changing snow conditions noted as a watch-out item
weather.probability: North Cascades alpine weather can shift quickly even in summer; changing snow conditions are a primary concern

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Consequential: remote location (existing hazards flags 'remoteness'), loose rock on Class 4 terrain, and long/complex approach mean a fall or injury carries serious self-rescue and evacuation implications

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer route (no NWAC zone specifically covers the remote Picket Range interior; nearest general NWAC coverage is the West Slopes North zone, but NWAC forecasts run winter/spring only and do not apply to this Jul-Sep climbing season)

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: Route crosses glacier/snow remnants on the approach and south side (per existing hazards: 'snow/glacier on approach'); crevasse hazard should be assumed present and evaluated in the field, though this is not a heavily glaciated route on the scale of larger North Cascades glaciers

road.name: North Cascades Highway (SR-20) to Ross Lake trailheads (via Ross Dam/water taxi) or the Access Creek/Thunder Creek trailheads near Diablo
road.status: SR-20 is paved and generally open in summer climbing season
road.driveNote: The Ross Lake Resort water taxi (about $35 one-way, cash, reservation recommended) cuts roughly 6 miles off the Big Beaver Trail approach; the Access Creek approach instead starts from a Thunder Creek-corridor trailhead off SR-20.
road.seasonalGate: SR-20 closes seasonally between Ross Lake and Mazama, typically mid-November through April/May depending on snowpack — check the WSDOT pass report before a shoulder-season trip

before.approach: Reaching Luna Cirque is the crux of the trip. The historical approach follows the Big Beaver Trail from Ross Lake (a $35 water taxi from Ross Lake Resort cuts about 6 miles off the hike) up to Luna Camp, then climbs steeply beside Luna Creek into the cirque — Fred Beckey himself described this bushwhack as 'the worst imaginable struggle with flies, devil's club, willows, and alder.' Most contemporary parties instead approach via Access Creek, which branches off that same Big Beaver Trail rather than a separate trailhead — parties continue on the maintained trail roughly 15-17.5 miles past Luna Camp to the unmarked Access Creek/Big Beaver Creek confluence, then leave the trail there to follow the Access Creek drainage (with an occasional bootpath) up into the cirque — a longer but far less brutal line than Luna Creek.
before.overview: The Luna Glacier route is Phantom Peak's original 1940 first-ascent line, named for the small hanging glacier that clings to the peak's east face above Luna Cirque (not an officially named glacier, but the moniker stuck). It's a moderate snow-and-easy-rock outing by Pickets standards — Grade II, Easy 5th class — but its remoteness and glacier crux keep it a rarely repeated route.
